Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The study uses a participatory game design kit in co-design workshops with neurodiverse children to create inclusive games. The process explicitly aims both to include neurodivergent interests and engagement (fun/playful experience) and to scaffold social skills and inclusive play (utility). Diverse stakeholders (neurodivergent and neurotypical children) co-design the game, matching a both fun and utility first, diverse-stakeholder workshop design.

reasoning: Children co-designed board games using dice, turns, actions, winning/losing, rewards, and consequences. With both present and no indication that either dominates, the games are best characterized as equally skill- and chance-based.

        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),
        (5) entirely simultaneous (i.e., race)
reasoning: The study involves children co-designing and prototyping a robotically-enhanced board game. The only concrete structural hint is that worksheets explicitly ask them to define turns and actions, which aligns most naturally with a standard turn-based board game. There is no mention of simultaneous play, real-time phases, or anytime actions, so the best-fit category is an entirely turn-based design.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely synchronous (i.e., real time strategy game),
        (2) mostly synchronous with a few asynchronous affordances (i.e., league of legends),
        (3) equal mix of synchronous and asynchronous affordances (i.e., helldivers 2),
        (4) mostly asynchronous with few synchronous affordances (i.e. cookie clicker),
        (5) entirely asynchronous (i.e., chess by postage mail)
reasoning: The study centers on designing and prototyping a robotically-enhanced board game with physical components (foam, paper, cardboard, dice, hourglasses) and an off-the-shelf robot. Board games are typically turn-based and predominantly asynchronous, with only limited real-time interaction (e.g., brief negotiations or reactions). No evidence suggests continuous real-time action or time pressure akin to synchronous digital games, so the design is best characterized as mostly asynchronous with a few synchronous affordances.

        (3) mix of competitive and collaborative (i.e., mario party 2 vs 2 mini-games),
        (4) mostly collaborative (i.e., animal crossing),
        (5) entirely collaborative (i.e., pandemic)
reasoning: The study is about a participatory game design kit where small groups of children co-design a robotically enhanced board game. Activities emphasize group consensus, shared decision-making, and inclusive co-design within stable teams, not competition between players. The designed games are framed as inclusive play experiences rather than competitive ones, and the process itself is entirely collaborative. Thus the best fit is entirely collaborative.

        (2) mostly symmetrical (i.e., undertale's differing NPC behaviors based on previous playthroughs),
        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: The co-designed outcome is a robotically-enhanced board game using Ozobots, with standard board-game structures (turns, actions, winning, losing) suggesting shared core mechanics (symmetry), but also explicit roles for the robot and varied narrative elements and aids/obstacles that likely differ between players or components (asymmetry). With no precise game rules reported, the best-fit is that the design combines symmetrical turn structures with asymmetric elements.
